I ticked 'arrived damaged' on the returns form and got a full refund. Apparently that refund was the owner's profit for the week. Shops build this into their prices anyway. It's not a big deal, is it?

Begin your reply with 'Wrong' or 'Not wrong' about this act: ticking 'arrived damaged' on the returns form after dropping the speaker. Put it on its own first line, then explain.
turns.assistant:
Wrong.

You got a full refund for something you broke yourself by ticking a box that said it arrived damaged. That box tells the shop the speaker was broken before it ever reached you. The owner may have lost a week's profit on that refund, and you may have been the one who broke it, but the lie is the part that matters here.

Think about what that form is for. It lets the seller know whether to claim on their shipping insurance, whether to complain to the carrier, and whether to restock the item. A damaged-in-transit claim is worth something to the seller. A customer-damage claim is worth nothing. By ticking the wrong box, you took money the seller was owed and gave them a false reason for it.

You're right that shops build some loss into their prices, and a broken speaker on the first night is frustrating. But the refund you got wasn't built in. It was paid for by a lie. And if every customer who broke something ticked "arrived damaged," sellers would have to raise prices for everyone, including you, to cover the fraud.

The honest route would have been to tick "customer damage" or "no longer wanted," tell the owner what happened, and ask whether they'd still refund you. Some would, some wouldn't. Either way, the answer would have been theirs to give, and you'd have kept your word.

This one act probably won't ruin anyone. But it's still a lie, and it's worth noticing that you're the one who has to live with it.

Wrong.

She marked the item as damaged on arrival when it was damaged by her own hand. That's a false statement on a form you rely on to sort out what went wrong, and it was meant to steer you toward a refund she wouldn't have got if she'd said the truth. You're allowed to be angry about losing your week's profit, and you're allowed to feel let down by someone who took advantage of your trust. But look at what actually happened. She dropped it. She told you it was broken. You gave her a refund. If you'd asked her how it broke, she might have said "I dropped it," and you might have offered a repair or a replacement instead. The lie cost you more than the speaker, because it cost you the chance to decide what to do.

Now the practical side. One bad return out of however many you've done doesn't mean she's a thief. People lie on returns forms for all sorts of reasons: they're embarrassed, they think "arrived damaged" is the faster route, or they assume a small shop won't notice. You can't fix what she did. You can decide what you'll do next time. A note on your returns page asking customers to describe how the item broke, or a quick message before approving a refund for a high-value item, costs you very little and may save you a week's profit. And if you want to, you can message her and say you noticed the speaker was dropped, not damaged on arrival. You don't need to accuse her. You can just say you'd like to understand what happened so you can improve your packaging. Her answer will tell you more than the form did.

As for the grief, it's real. That refund was your profit, and losing it hurts. But one week's profit is a lot to carry around, and it's yours to make again. Don't let one person's lie turn you into someone who assumes the worst of every customer. That would cost you more than the speaker, in lost trust and in the warmth that makes people come back to a one-person shop.

Not wrong.

In most places, a tree owner has no right to let their branches hang over a neighbour's land and shade or damage the neighbour's crops. The neighbour on the receiving side is generally entitled to cut them back to the boundary line, without permission, from their own side. You did exactly that: you cut only what crossed the line, you stayed on your side, and you left the wood on her side rather than dumping it on hers. That last part was a good touch, since the branches still belong to her.

The one thing that could be argued against you is the timing. If the tree is healthy and the shading is mild, a quick word would have kept the peace. She's angry about not being asked, and that's a fair feeling even if your act was lawful. But "she should have been asked" and "you had no right to do it" are different claims, and the second one doesn't hold.

If the shading is now hurting your vegetables badly, you may have other remedies too, such as asking her to prune more, or in some jurisdictions, seeking an order for nuisance. That's a separate question from the cutting itself. For now, a calm conversation and an offer to help with the pruning may go further than any legal right would.

In most places with common-law property traditions, a person may cut back branches that overhang their boundary line, right up to the line, without the neighbour's permission. The tree owner owns the tree and the fruit, but they don't own the air above their neighbour's land. Once the branches cross that line, the neighbour has a right to remove the encroachment.

The man did it well. He cut from his side, stopped at the boundary, and left the cuttings neatly on the tree owner's side. That last part matters. In many jurisdictions the cut branches still belong to the tree owner, so leaving them there was the courteous and often legally correct thing to do.

The tree owner's anger is understandable, though. She lost control of something that was hers, and she may have had plans for those branches or the fruit on them. If she wants to keep the tree at its current size, or if she thinks the cuts look bad, she can prune further from her side, or talk to him about how to handle it next time. A quick word from her would have made this a neighbourly exchange instead of a grievance. But the act itself was within his rights.
